claim: Sleep duration is significantly reduced in Pachón cavefish compared to surface morph.
source: Sleep duration is significantly reduced in Pachón cavefish compared to surface morph (Unpaired t-test, t = 5.56, n = 26, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of behavioral data comparing sleep duration between surface fish and Pachón cavefish, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of hcrt normalized by GAPDH in adult whole-brain extracts is significantly enhanced in Pachón cavefish compared to surface fish.
source: Expression of hcrt normalized by GAPDH in adult whole-brain extracts is significantly enhanced in Pachón cavefish compared to surface fish (Unpaired t-test, t = 11.15, n = 8, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by qPCR measurements of hcrt transcript levels in whole-brain extracts, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HCRT neuropeptide signal is significantly increased in Pachón cavefish compared to surface fish.
source: HCRT neuropeptide signal is significantly increased in Pachón cavefish compared to surface fish (Unpaired t-test, t = 5.94, n = 8, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification of HCRT fluorescence intensity in brain sections, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The number of HCRT-positive cells in the hypothalamus is significantly increased in cavefish compared to surface fish.
source: The number of HCRT-positive cells in the hypothalamus is significantly increased in cavefish compared to surface fish (Unpaired t-test, t = 9.984, n = 8, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by cell counting from immunostained brain sections, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A. mexicanus shares high sequence similarity to other fish species (35–48% percent identity) and mammals (35% percent identity) for the HCRT neuropeptide.
source: Alignment of the HCRT neuropeptide reveals that A. mexicanus shares high sequence similarity to other fish species (35–48% percent identity) and mammals (35% percent identity), including conservation of domains that give rise to the HCRT neuropeptides (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The HCRT peptide sequences of surface and Pachón cavefish are identical (100% percent identity).
source: The HCRT peptide sequences of surface and Pachón cavefish are identical (100% percent identity).
evidence: Stated based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Expression of the housekeeping gene GAPDH was comparable between both forms.
source: Expression of the housekeeping gene, GAPDH, was comparable between both forms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Enhanced levels of HCRT protein were observed in five day post fertilization (dpf) larvae.
source: Enhanced levels of HCRT protein were also observed in five day post fertilization (dpf) larvae, suggesting the change in peptide levels were present at the time fish begin consuming food (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in larval fish shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: HCRT neuropeptide levels are significantly increased in five dpf Pachón larvae compared to surface.
source: HCRT neuropeptide levels are significantly increased in five dpf Pachón larvae compared to surface (Unpaired t-test, t = 3.17, df = 10, p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by quantification of HCRT immunofluorescence in larval fish, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The cavefish and surface fish genomes encode only HCRTR2.
source: We performed genome analysis to explore how many paralog HCRTR genes resided in the genome of A. mexicanus, and found the cavefish and surface fish genomes encode only HCRTR2 (McGaugh et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by genome analysis with citation to McGaugh et al., 2014.

claim: Treatment of TCSOX229 in Pachón cavefish increased sleep duration compared to solvent treated (DMSO) controls.
source: Conversely, treatment of TCSOX229 in Pachón cavefish increased sleep duration compared to solvent treated (DMSO) controls (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from pharmacological treatment experiments shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Sleep in surface fish remained unchanged in the presence of 1 μM or 10 μM TCSOX229.
source: Sleep in surface fish remained unchanged in the presence of 1 μM or 10 μM TCSOX229 (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from pharmacological treatment experiments shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: Treatment with TCSOX229 had no effect on waking velocity in surface fish or cavefish.
source: Treatment with TCSOX229 had no effect on waking velocity in surface fish or cavefish, suggesting that the increased quiescence observed in cavefish after drug treatment is not due to lethargy (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral analysis of waking activity shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Sleep-promoting effects of TCSOX229 in cavefish can be attributed to both an increase in bout number and bout duration.
source: Further analysis revealed that sleep-promoting effects of TCSOX229 in cavefish can be attributed to both an increase in bout number and bout duration, suggesting that HCRT blockade affects sleep onset and maintenance (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sleep architecture parameters shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Pachón cavefish treated with 10 μM TCS significantly increased sleep compared to control treated fish.
source: Pachón cavefish teated with 1 μM TCS trended towards increased sleep (p>0.178, n = 12) while treatment with 10 μM significantly increased sleep (p<0.01, n = 13; F(1, 73)=25.00,) compared to control treated fish.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of sleep duration data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Treatment with 10 μM TCS significantly increased bout duration in Pachón cavefish.
source: Treatment of Pachón cavefish with 1 μM TCS trended towards increased bout duration, p>0.051, n = 12, while 10 μM TCS treatment significantly increased bout duration in Pachón cavefish, (p<0.01, n = 13; F(1, 73)=47.42).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of sleep bout duration shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Treatment with 10 μM TCS significantly increased bout number in Pachón cavefish.
source: Treatment with 10 μM TCS significantly increased bout duration in Pachón cavefish,(p<0.001, n = 13; 2-way ANOVA, F(1, 68)=3.309).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of sleep bout number shown in Figure 2F.

claim: None of the three HCRT antagonists altered sleep in surface fish.
source: None of the three antagonists altered sleep in surface fish, whereas they significantly increased sleep in cavefish (Figure 3B) at this concentration.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from pharmacological treatment with three different HCRT antagonists shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All three HCRT antagonists significantly increased sleep in cavefish at 30 µM concentration.
source: None of the three antagonists altered sleep in surface fish, whereas they significantly increased sleep in cavefish (Figure 3B) at this concentration.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from pharmacological treatment shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The waking activity was not affected by antagonist treatment in surface fish or cavefish.
source: The waking activity was not affected by antagonist treatment in surface fish or cavefish, supporting the notion that the sleep promoting effects on cavefish are not due to induction of lethargy (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of waking activity shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All three HCRT antagonists significantly increased sleep bout number in cavefish.
source: Further, all three HCRT antagonists significantly increased sleep bout number, and bout duration in cavefish (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sleep architecture shown in Figure 3D.

claim: All three HCRT antagonists significantly increased sleep bout duration in cavefish.
source: Further, all three HCRT antagonists significantly increased sleep bout number, and bout duration in cavefish (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sleep architecture shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Treatment with YNT-185 significantly reduced sleep in surface fish.
source: Treatment with YNT-185 significantly reduced sleep in surface fish, without affecting sleep in cavefish where HCRT levels are naturally elevated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 ).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from HCRTR2 agonist treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with YNT-185 did not affect sleep in cavefish.
source: Treatment with YNT-185 significantly reduced sleep in surface fish, without affecting sleep in cavefish where HCRT levels are naturally elevated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 ).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from HCRTR2 agonist treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activity during waking bouts was not significantly altered with treatment of YNT-185 in either surface or Pachón cavefish.
source: Activity during waking bouts was not significantly altered with treatment of YNT-185 in either surface or Pachón cavefish, suggesting that the reduction in total sleep of surface fish was not due to lethargy.
evidence: Supported by analysis of waking activity shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: YNT-185 treatment significantly reduced the total number of sleep bouts in surface fish.
source: Further, YNT-185 treatment significantly reduced the total number of sleep bouts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sleep bout number shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At four dpf, sleep in Pachón cavefish is significantly reduced compared to surface fish that were age-matched.
source: We found that at four dpf, sleep in Pachón cavefish is significantly reduced compared to surface fish that were age-matched (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in larval fish shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Injection of 0.2 mM hcrt MO enhanced sleep in cavefish compared to fish injected with scrambled MO control.
source: Injection of 0.2 mM hcrt MO enhanced sleep in cavefish compared to fish injected with scrambled MO control, whereas knock-down of hcrt using the same MO had no observable effect on surface fish (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Knock-down of hcrt using morpholino had no observable effect on surface fish sleep.
source: Injection of 0.2 mM hcrt MO enhanced sleep in cavefish compared to fish injected with scrambled MO control, whereas knock-down of hcrt using the same MO had no observable effect on surface fish (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The mortality of fish injected with 0.2 mM hcrt MOs, 0.2 mM scramble MOs, and non-injected controls did not differ.
source: The mortality of fish injected with 0.2 mM hcrt MOs, 0.2 mM scramble MOs, and non-injected controls did not differ, indicating at the concentration used, there is no generalized effect of injection procedure or MO treatment on survival (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Morpholino treatment did not affect activity during wake bouts in surface fish or Pachón cavefish.
source: Morpholino treatment did not affect activity during wake bouts in surface fish or Pachón cavefish (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of waking activity shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Injection of 0.2 mM hcrt MO increased total sleep bout number in Pachón cavefish.
source: Analysis of sleep architecture revealed that injection of 0.2 mM hcrt MO increased total sleep bout number and sleep bout duration in Pachón cavefish, though not to levels of surface fish(Figure 4C; Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sleep architecture shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Injection of 0.2 mM hcrt MO increased sleep bout duration in Pachón cavefish.
source: Analysis of sleep architecture revealed that injection of 0.2 mM hcrt MO increased total sleep bout number and sleep bout duration in Pachón cavefish, though not to levels of surface fish(Figure 4C; Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sleep architecture shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All GFP-positive neurons were co-labeled by Anti-HCRT.
source: Further, all GFP-positive neurons were co-labeled by Anti-HCRT, demonstrating that this approach specifically targets BoTXBLC transgene expression to HCRT neurons (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry showing colocalization of GFP and HCRT in Figure 5B,D.

claim: Sleep was significantly increased in experimental double transgenic Pachón cavefish (hcrt:GAL4:UAS-BoTxTxBLC-GFP) compared to both control groups.
source: Sleep was significantly increased in experimental double transgenic Pachón cavefish (hcrt:GAL4:UAS-BoTxTxBLC-GFP) compared to both control groups, while there was no effect in surface fish (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from genetic silencing experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Genetic silencing of HCRT neurons had no effect on sleep in surface fish.
source: Sleep was significantly increased in experimental double transgenic Pachón cavefish (hcrt:GAL4:UAS-BoTxTxBLC-GFP) compared to both control groups, while there was no effect in surface fish (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from genetic silencing experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Waking velocity in surface fish and cavefish was not changed between both control groups and fish expressing hcrt:GAL4; UAS-BoTxBLC-GFP.
source: Waking velocity in surface fish and cavefish was not changed between both control groups and fish expressing hcrt:GAL4; UAS-BoTxBLC-GFP, suggesting that the increased quiescence from neuronal silencing is not due to lethargy (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of waking activity shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Silencing subsets of HCRT neurons increased sleep in Pachón cavefish by increasing bout number without affecting bout duration.
source: Silencing subsets of HCRT neurons increased sleep in Pachón cavefish by increasing bout number (Figure 5A–S) without affecting bout duration (Figure 5B–S).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sleep architecture shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Regression analysis of the number of neurons silenced significantly correlated with total sleep duration (R2 = 0.229) in Pachón cavefish.
source: Regression analysis of the number of neurons silenced significantly correlated with total sleep duration (R2 = 0.229) in Pachón cavefish, fortifying the notion that increased HCRT signaling is associated with sleep loss (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A weak correlation between BoTX-expressing HCRT neurons and sleep duration (R2 = 0.091) was observed in surface fish.
source: A weak correlation between BoTX-expressing HCRT neurons and sleep duration (R2 = 0.091) was also observed in surface fish Figure 5G, consistent with the notion that HCRT may also regulates sleep in surface fish, but cavefish are more sensitive to subtle changes of HCRT signaling.
evidence: Supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Gentamicin treatment fully ablated the lateral line.
source: In agreement with previous findings, gentamicin treatment fully ablated the lateral line (Figure 6A–D) and restored sleep in cavefish without affecting sleep in surface fish (Jaggard et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by DASPEI staining shown in Figure 6A–D and cited previous findings.

claim: Gentamicin treatment restored sleep in cavefish without affecting sleep in surface fish.
source: In agreement with previous findings, gentamicin treatment fully ablated the lateral line (Figure 6A–D) and restored sleep in cavefish without affecting sleep in surface fish (Jaggard et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citation to previous findings (Jaggard et al., 2017).

claim: Gentamicin treatment significantly reduced hcrt expression in cavefish to levels equivalent to untreated surface fish.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis of gentamicin treatment revealed that hcrt expression was significantly reduced in cavefish to levels equivalent to untreated surface fish (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There were no significant changes in hcrt expression following gentamicin treatment in surface fish.
source: By contrast, there were no significant changes in hcrt expression following gentamicin treatment in surface fish.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Lateral line ablation does not impact the number of HCRT-positive hypothalamic neurons.
source: Comparison and detailed quantification of HCRT neuropeptide levels in the hypothalamus reveals that lateral line ablation does not impact the number of HCRT-positive hypothalamic neurons, but instead selectively reduces the level of HCRT within each cell in cavefish (Figure 6F–K), supporting the notion that the lateral line is required for enhancement of HCRT function in cavefish.
evidence: Supported by quantification of HCRT-positive cells shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Lateral line ablation selectively reduces the level of HCRT within each cell in cavefish.
source: Comparison and detailed quantification of HCRT neuropeptide levels in the hypothalamus reveals that lateral line ablation does not impact the number of HCRT-positive hypothalamic neurons, but instead selectively reduces the level of HCRT within each cell in cavefish (Figure 6F–K), supporting the notion that the lateral line is required for enhancement of HCRT function in cavefish.
evidence: Supported by quantification of HCRT fluorescence intensity shown in Figure 6F.

claim: hcrt transcript is significantly reduced in cavefish following 30 days of starvation.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis from whole-brain extracts revealed that hcrt transcript is significantly reduced in cavefish following 30 days of starvation; however, the same treatment does not affect hcrt transcription in surface fish, indicating that cavefish are more sensitive to starvation-dependent changes in HCRT (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Starvation does not affect hcrt transcription in surface fish.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis from whole-brain extracts revealed that hcrt transcript is significantly reduced in cavefish following 30 days of starvation; however, the same treatment does not affect hcrt transcription in surface fish, indicating that cavefish are more sensitive to starvation-dependent changes in HCRT (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Starvation reduced HCRT levels in each cell, without affecting the number of HCRT-positive neurons.
source: Similar to lateral line ablation, starvation reduced HCRT levels in each cell, without affecting the number of HCRT-positive neurons.
evidence: Supported by quantification of HCRT immunofluorescence shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: Starvation did not affect the number of HCRT-positive cells or HCRT levels per cell in surface fish.
source: Further, starvation did not affect the number of HCRT-positive cells or HCRT levels per cell in surface fish (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of HCRT immunofluorescence shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: Astyanax mexicanus consists of eyed surface populations that inhabit rivers in the Sierra del Abra region of Northeast Mexico, and at least 29 distinct populations of cavefish in this region.
source: Astyanax mexicanus consists of eyed surface populations that inhabit rivers in the Sierra del Abra region of Northeast Mexico, and at least 29 distinct populations of cavefish in this region (Mitchell et al., 1977).
evidence: Stated with citation to Mitchell et al., 1977.

claim: Cavefish are derived from surface ancestors, which arose from colonization events that are estimated to have taken place within the past 2–5 million years.
source: Cavefish are derived from surface ancestors, which arose from colonization events that are estimated to have taken place within the past 2–5 million years (Gross, 2012; Jeffery, 2009; Keene et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citations to Gross, 2012; Jeffery, 2009; Keene et al., 2015.

claim: Independently-evolved cave populations of A. mexicanus share morphological and developmental phenotypes including smaller or completely absent eyes, and loss of pigmentation.
source: Independently-evolved cave populations of A. mexicanus share morphological and developmental phenotypes including smaller or completely absent eyes, and loss of pigmentation (Borowsky, 2008a; Gross and Wilkens, 2013; Protas et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated with citations to Borowsky, 2008a; Gross and Wilkens, 2013; Protas et al., 2006.

claim: Cavefish display an array of behavioral changes including reduced schooling, enhanced vibration attraction behavior, hyperphagia, and sleep loss.
source: In addition, cavefish display an array of behavioral changes including reduced schooling, enhanced vibration attraction behavior, hyperphagia, and sleep loss (Aspiras et al., 2015; Duboué et al., 2011; Kowalko et al., 2013; Yoshizawa et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated with citations to Aspiras et al., 2015; Duboué et al., 2011; Kowalko et al., 2013; Yoshizawa et al., 2010.

claim: Relative to extant conspecifics that inhabit caves, independently derived cave-dwelling populations display a striking 80% reduction in total sleep with no adverse impacts on health or development.
source: Relative to extant conspecifics that inhabit caves, independently derived cave-dwelling populations display a striking 80% reduction in total sleep with no adverse impacts on health or development (Duboué et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated with citation to Duboué et al., 2011.

claim: Many cave waters inhabited by A. mexicanus are nutrient poor compared to the above-ground rivers surrounding them.
source: Many cave waters inhabited by A. mexicanus are nutrient poor compared to the above-ground rivers surrounding them (Mitchell et al., 1977), and previous field studies suggest cavefish subsist primarily off of bat guano, small insects, and organic matter washed into the cave by seasonal floods (Keene et al., 2015; Mitchell et al., 1977).
evidence: Stated with citations to Mitchell et al., 1977; Keene et al., 2015.

claim: Following starvation, cave-derived fish have a slower rate of weight loss compared to surface conspecific.
source: Following starvation, cave-derived fish have a slower rate of weight loss compared to surface conspecific, suggesting that a reduced metabolism may account, in part, for adaptation to cave life (Aspiras et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citation to Aspiras et al., 2015.

claim: Sleep is increased in cavefish during periods of prolonged starvation.
source: We previously found that sleep is increased in cavefish during periods of prolonged starvation, raising the possibility that cavefish suppress sleep to forage during the wet season when food is plentiful, and increase sleep to conserve energy during the dry season when food is less abundant (Jaggard et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citation to Jaggard et al., 2017.

claim: Many behaviors that are altered in cavefish are regulated by the hypothalamus, which is enlarged in cavefish.
source: Many behaviors that are altered in cavefish are regulated by the hypothalamus, which is enlarged in cavefish (Menuet et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated with citation to Menuet et al., 2007.

claim: Deficiencies in HCRT signaling are associated with altered sleep and narcolepsy-associated phenotypes in diverse vertebrate organisms.
source: Deficiencies in HCRT signaling are associated with altered sleep and narcolepsy-associated phenotypes in diverse vertebrate organisms (Appelbaum et al., 2009; Chemelli et al., 1999; Faraco et al., 2006; Lin et al., 1999; Prober et al., 2006; Yokogawa et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: In zebrafish, HCRT is critical for normal sleep-wake regulation.
source: In zebrafish, HCRT is critical for normal sleep-wake regulation. Ectopic expression of hcrt increases locomotor activity, while ablation of HCRT neurons increases daytime sleep (Elbaz et al., 2012; Prober et al., 2006; Singh et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citations to Elbaz et al., 2012; Prober et al., 2006; Singh et al., 2015.

claim: Ablation of the lateral line restores sleep to Pachón cavefish without affecting sleep in surface fish.
source: We previously reported that ablation of the lateral line restores sleep to Pachón cavefish without affecting sleep in surface fish, raising the possibility that lateral line input modulates HCRT signaling in cavefish to suppress sleep (Jaggard et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citation to Jaggard et al., 2017.

claim: The number of mechanosensory neuromasts that comprise the lateral line are increased in cavefish.
source: The number of mechanosensory neuromasts that comprise the lateral line, a neuromodulatory system used to detect prey and water flow, are increased in cavefish. This evolved trait is hypothesized to allow for an enhanced ability to forage, object detection, and social behaviors in the absence of eyes (Kowalko et al., 2013; Kulpa et al., 2015; Yoshizawa et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated with citations to Kowalko et al., 2013; Kulpa et al., 2015; Yoshizawa et al., 2010.

claim: Mammals possess two HCRT receptors (HCRTR1 and HCRTR2).
source: While mammals possess two HCRT receptors (HCRTR1 and HCRTR2), zebrafish only possess HCRTR2 (Prober et al., 2006; Yokogawa et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated with citations to Prober et al., 2006; Yokogawa et al., 2007.

claim: Zebrafish only possess HCRTR2.
source: While mammals possess two HCRT receptors (HCRTR1 and HCRTR2), zebrafish only possess HCRTR2 (Prober et al., 2006; Yokogawa et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated with citations to Prober et al., 2006; Yokogawa et al., 2007.

claim: HCRTR2 is proposed to be evolutionarily more ancient compared to HCRTR1.
source: Importantly, HCRTR2 is proposed to be evolutionarily more ancient compared to HCRTR1 (Wong et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated with citation to Wong et al., 2011.

claim: Sleep loss in A. mexicanus cavefish populations is found across developmental stages, from larval and juvenile forms to adults.
source: Sleep loss in A. mexicanus cavefish populations is found across developmental stages, from larval and juvenile forms to adults (Duboué et al., 2011; Yoshizawa et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citations to Duboué et al., 2011; Yoshizawa et al., 2015.

claim: HCRT neurons are modulated by sensory stimuli and feeding state.
source: Hypocretin neurons are modulated by sensory stimuli and feeding state, indicating that they are involved in the integration of environmental cues with sleep regulation (Appelbaum et al., 2007; Mileykovskiy et al., 2005).
evidence: Stated with citations to Appelbaum et al., 2007; Mileykovskiy et al., 2005.

claim: In mice, HCRT neurons are transiently activated by sound, feeding, and cage exploration.
source: In mice, HCRT neurons are transiently activated by sound, feeding, and cage exploration, suggesting that HCRT neurons are generally regulated by external stimuli (Mileykovskiy et al., 2005).
evidence: Stated with citation to Mileykovskiy et al., 2005.

claim: In zebrafish, HCRT neurons activation is associated with periods of wakefulness.
source: Further in zebrafish, HCRT neurons activation is associated with periods of wakefulness and overexpression of HCRT enhances locomotor response to diverse sensory stimuli, while ablation of HCRT neurons reduces response to sound stimulus (Elbaz et al., 2012; Naumann et al., 2010; Prober et al., 2006; Woods et al., 2014), suggesting that HCRT neurons mediate sensory responsiveness and sleep-wake behavior.
evidence: Stated with citations to Elbaz et al., 2012; Naumann et al., 2010; Prober et al., 2006; Woods et al., 2014.

claim: Overexpression of HCRT enhances locomotor response to diverse sensory stimuli in zebrafish.
source: Further in zebrafish, HCRT neurons activation is associated with periods of wakefulness and overexpression of HCRT enhances locomotor response to diverse sensory stimuli, while ablation of HCRT neurons reduces response to sound stimulus (Elbaz et al., 2012; Naumann et al., 2010; Prober et al., 2006; Woods et al., 2014), suggesting that HCRT neurons mediate sensory responsiveness and sleep-wake behavior.
evidence: Stated with citations to Elbaz et al., 2012; Naumann et al., 2010; Prober et al., 2006; Woods et al., 2014.

claim: Ablation of HCRT neurons reduces response to sound stimulus in zebrafish.
source: Further in zebrafish, HCRT neurons activation is associated with periods of wakefulness and overexpression of HCRT enhances locomotor response to diverse sensory stimuli, while ablation of HCRT neurons reduces response to sound stimulus (Elbaz et al., 2012; Naumann et al., 2010; Prober et al., 2006; Woods et al., 2014), suggesting that HCRT neurons mediate sensory responsiveness and sleep-wake behavior.
evidence: Stated with citations to Elbaz et al., 2012; Naumann et al., 2010; Prober et al., 2006; Woods et al., 2014.

claim: HCRT neurons send projections to numerous areas implicated in behavioral regulation including the periventricular hypothalamus, the raphe, and thalamic nuclei.
source: While a full understanding of the neural circuitry regulating HCRT-positive neurons has not been determined, HCRT neurons send projections to numerous areas implicated in behavioral regulation including the periventricular hypothalamus, the raphe, and thalamic nuclei (Panula, 2010).
evidence: Stated with citation to Panula, 2010.

claim: The wake-consolidating role of HCRT neurons is dependent on norepinephrine signaling.
source: Evidence suggests that the wake-consolidating role of HCRT neurons is dependent on norepinephrine signaling, and optogenetic activation of HCRT neurons activates the locus coeruleus (Singh et al., 2015), raising the possibility that activation of this arousal pathway is enhanced in Pachón cavefish.
evidence: Stated with citation to Singh et al., 2015.

claim: Optogenetic activation of HCRT neurons activates the locus coeruleus.
source: Evidence suggests that the wake-consolidating role of HCRT neurons is dependent on norepinephrine signaling, and optogenetic activation of HCRT neurons activates the locus coeruleus (Singh et al., 2015), raising the possibility that activation of this arousal pathway is enhanced in Pachón cavefish.
evidence: Stated with citation to Singh et al., 2015.

claim: Norepinephrine levels are elevated in the brains of cavefish.
source: Norepinephrine levels are elevated in the brains of cavefish and treatment of cavefish with the β-adrenergic inhibitor propranolol restores sleep in cavefish without affecting sleep in surface fish. (Bilandžija et al., 2013; Duboué et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citations to Bilandžija et al., 2013; Duboué et al., 2012.

claim: Treatment of cavefish with the β-adrenergic inhibitor propranolol restores sleep in cavefish without affecting sleep in surface fish.
source: Norepinephrine levels are elevated in the brains of cavefish and treatment of cavefish with the β-adrenergic inhibitor propranolol restores sleep in cavefish without affecting sleep in surface fish. (Bilandžija et al., 2013; Duboué et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citations to Bilandžija et al., 2013; Duboué et al., 2012.

claim: Injection of HCRT peptide increases food consumption in cavefish.
source: Previous findings reveal that injection of HCRT peptide increases food consumption in cavefish, suggesting the consummatory behavior induced by HCRT in mammals is conserved in A. mexicanus (Penney and Volkoff, 2014; Wall and Volkoff, 2013).
evidence: Stated with citations to Penney and Volkoff, 2014; Wall and Volkoff, 2013.

claim: HCRT neurons are regulated by the adipose peptide hormone, Leptin in mammals and zebrafish.
source: Studies in mammals and zebrafish suggest HCRT neurons are regulated by the adipose peptide hormone, Leptin (Leinninger et al., 2011; Levitas-Djerbi et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citations to Leinninger et al., 2011; Levitas-Djerbi et al., 2015.

claim: Adipose levels in cavefish are elevated compared to surface fish.
source: Adipose levels in cavefish are elevated compared to surface fish (Aspiras et al., 2015), and it is possible that prolonged starvation reduces Leptin levels, thereby inhibiting hcrt expression to promote sleep in cavefish.
evidence: Stated with citation to Aspiras et al., 2015.

claim: Evolved differences in the lateral line system have been identified between surface fish and cavefish.
source: Further, the lateral line system is intimately linked to feeding behavior in fish, and evolved differences in the lateral line system have been identified between surface fish and cavefish (Yoshizawa et al., 2012), perhaps including increased modulation of hcrt neurons.
evidence: Stated with citation to Yoshizawa et al., 2012.

claim: Convergent evolution of sleep loss has been demonstrated in other populations of cavefish, including Molino, Tinaja and Chica cave populations.
source: We have also demonstrated evolutionary convergence on sleep loss in other populations of cavefish, including Molino, Tinaja and Chica cave populations (Jaggard et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citation to Jaggard et al., 2017.

claim: Ablation of the lateral line has no effect on sleep in Molino, Tinaja and Chica populations.
source: However, ablation of the lateral line has no effect on sleep in Molino, Tinaja and Chica populations, suggesting distinct neural mechanism underlie sleep loss between Pachón cavefish, and other cavefish populations assayed (Jaggard et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citation to Jaggard et al., 2017.

claim: Both morphological and genomic data suggest Pachón cavefish are one of the oldest, and most troglomorphic of the 29 A. mexicanus cavefish populations.
source: Both morphological and genomic data suggest Pachón cavefish are one of the oldest, and most troglomorphic of the 29 A. mexicanus cavefish populations (Bradic et al., 2012; Dowling et al., 2002; Ornelas-García et al., 2008; Strecker et al., 2003).
evidence: Stated with citations to Bradic et al., 2012; Dowling et al., 2002; Ornelas-García et al., 2008; Strecker et al., 2003.

claim: Increased levels of the homeobox transcription factor Lhx9 specifies greater number of HCRT-neurons in cavefish.
source: These observations are in agreement with concurrent findings that increased levels of the homeobox transcription factor Lhx9 specifies greater number of HCRT-neurons in cavefish (Alie et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citation to Alie et al., 2018.

claim: Neurons expressing Neuropeptide Y are increased in cavefish.
source: A concurrent paper revealed that neurons expressing Neuropeptide Y are also increased in cavefish (Alie et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citation to Alie et al., 2018.

claim: Neuropeptide Y regulates feeding and sleep in diverse species.
source: Like Hcrt, Neuropeptide Y also regulates feeding and sleep in diverse species, suggesting changes in hypothalamic regulation of sleep are, at least partially, developmentally-derived and not limited to the changes in Hcrt function that we have observed (Chung et al., 2017; Luquet et al., 2005; Szentirmai and Krueger, 2006; Wu et al., 2003).
evidence: Stated with citations to Chung et al., 2017; Luquet et al., 2005; Szentirmai and Krueger, 2006; Wu et al., 2003.

claim: Hypocretin is highly conserved and has been shown to consolidate wakefulness in species ranging from zebrafish to humans.
source: Indeed, Hypocretin is highly conserved and has been shown to consolidate wakefulness in species including in animals ranging from zebrafish to humans (Appelbaum et al., 2009; Chemelli et al., 1999; Mileykovskiy et al., 2005; Prober et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated with citations to Appelbaum et al., 2009; Chemelli et al., 1999; Mileykovskiy et al., 2005; Prober et al., 2006.

claim: The Hypocretin system has been characterized in detail in zebrafish and acts as a key mediator of arousal.
source: Moreover, the Hypocretin system has been characterized in detail in zebrafish and acts as a key mediator of arousal (Appelbaum et al., 2009; Elbaz et al., 2012; Kaslin et al., 2004; Prober et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated with citations to Appelbaum et al., 2009; Elbaz et al., 2012; Kaslin et al., 2004; Prober et al., 2006.

claim: Enhanced HCRT signaling underlies the evolution of sleep loss in Mexican cavefish.
source: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of HCRT signaling increases sleep in cavefish, suggesting enhanced HCRT signaling underlies the evolution of sleep loss.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental manipulations (pharmacological and genetic) showing that inhibiting HCRT increases sleep in cavefish.

claim: Ablation of the lateral line or starvation inhibit hcrt expression in cavefish while having little effect on surface fish.
source: Ablation of the lateral line or starvation, manipulations that selectively promote sleep in cavefish, inhibit hcrt expression in cavefish while having little effect on surface fish.
evidence: Supported by qPCR and immunohistochemistry data showing differential effects of these manipulations on hcrt expression between surface fish and cavefish.

claim: The findings provide the first evidence of genetic and neuronal changes that contribute to the evolution of sleep loss.
source: These findings provide the first evidence of genetic and neuronal changes that contribute to the evolution of sleep loss, and support a conserved role for HCRT in sleep regulation.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: The findings support a conserved role for HCRT in sleep regulation.
source: These findings provide the first evidence of genetic and neuronal changes that contribute to the evolution of sleep loss, and support a conserved role for HCRT in sleep regulation.
evidence: Based on the demonstration that HCRT regulates sleep in cavefish, consistent with its known role in other species.

claim: Upregulation of hcrt underlies the evolution of sleep loss in cavefish.
source: By contrast, hcrt expression was significantly elevated in Pachón cavefish to over three-fold the levels of surface fish, raising the possibility that upregulation of hcrt underlies the evolution of sleep loss (Figure 1C).
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between elevated hcrt expression and sleep loss in cavefish, though causality is suggested rather than definitively proven.

claim: Cavefish are more sensitive to changes in HCRT signaling than surface fish.
source: The sleep-promoting effect of HCRT antagonists in Pachón cavefish suggests these fish are more sensitive to changes in HCRT signaling than surface fish.
evidence: Inferred from the differential response to HCRT antagonists between surface fish and cavefish.

claim: HCRT blockade affects sleep onset and maintenance in cavefish.
source: Further analysis revealed that sleep-promoting effects of TCSOX229 in cavefish can be attributed to both an increase in bout number and bout duration, suggesting that HCRT blockade affects sleep onset and maintenance (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both bout number (related to sleep onset) and bout duration (related to sleep maintenance) are affected.

claim: The lateral line is required for enhancement of HCRT function in cavefish.
source: Comparison and detailed quantification of HCRT neuropeptide levels in the hypothalamus reveals that lateral line ablation does not impact the number of HCRT-positive hypothalamic neurons, but instead selectively reduces the level of HCRT within each cell in cavefish (Figure 6F–K), supporting the notion that the lateral line is required for enhancement of HCRT function in cavefish.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that lateral line ablation reduces HCRT levels in cavefish.

claim: Sensory input from the lateral line promotes sleep and hcrt expression in Pachón cavefish.
source: Together, these findings reveal that sensory input from the lateral line promotes sleep and hcrt expression in Pachón cavefish, providing a link between sensory input and transcriptional regulation of a wake-promoting factor.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that lateral line ablation reduces hcrt expression and increases sleep in cavefish.

claim: Cavefish are more sensitive to starvation-dependent changes in HCRT.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis from whole-brain extracts revealed that hcrt transcript is significantly reduced in cavefish following 30 days of starvation; however, the same treatment does not affect hcrt transcription in surface fish, indicating that cavefish are more sensitive to starvation-dependent changes in HCRT (Figure 7A).
evidence: Inferred from the differential response to starvation between surface fish and cavefish.

claim: Starvation modulates HCRT levels, rather than the number of cells that produce HCRT.
source: These results indicate that the starvation modulates HCRT levels, rather than the number of cells that produce HCRT.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that starvation affects HCRT intensity per cell but not cell number.

claim: Developmentally-derived differences in the number of HCRT-positive neurons and modified hypothalamic neural circuitry contribute to sleep loss in cavefish.
source: Therefore, it is likely that developmentally-derived differences in the number of HCRT-positive neurons and modified hypothalamic neural circuitry contribute to sleep loss in cavefish.
evidence: Inferred from observations of increased HCRT neurons in early development and known hypothalamic differences.

claim: Regulation of HCRT signaling may be subject to evolutionary pressure.
source: The findings presented here extend studies in mammalian and zebrafish models, and suggest that regulation of HCRT signaling may be subject to evolutionary pressure, and implicate it as a potential 'hot-spot' for variation in sleep throughout the animal kingdom.
evidence: Inferred from the evolved differences in HCRT function between surface fish and cavefish.

claim: HCRT is a potential 'hot-spot' for variation in sleep throughout the animal kingdom.
source: The findings presented here extend studies in mammalian and zebrafish models, and suggest that regulation of HCRT signaling may be subject to evolutionary pressure, and implicate it as a potential 'hot-spot' for variation in sleep throughout the animal kingdom.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the findings in cavefish and known conservation of HCRT function.

claim: Evolution of sensory systems dramatically affect central brain processes that regulate behavior.
source: These findings support the notion that evolution of sensory systems dramatically affect central brain processes that regulate behavior, and provide further support that HCRT neurons integrate sensory stimuli to modulate sleep and arousal.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that lateral line input affects HCRT expression and sleep.

claim: HCRT neurons integrate sensory stimuli to modulate sleep and arousal.
source: These findings support the notion that evolution of sensory systems dramatically affect central brain processes that regulate behavior, and provide further support that HCRT neurons integrate sensory stimuli to modulate sleep and arousal.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that lateral line input affects HCRT expression and sleep, combined with cited literature.

claim: Differences in norepinephrine signaling may contribute to hcrt-dependent sleep loss in cavefish.
source: Therefore, it is possible that differences in norepinephrine signaling contribute to hcrt-dependent sleep loss in cavefish.
evidence: Speculative inference based on known interactions between HCRT and norepinephrine systems and elevated norepinephrine in cavefish.

claim: Prolonged starvation may reduce Leptin levels, thereby inhibiting hcrt expression to promote sleep in cavefish.
source: Adipose levels in cavefish are elevated compared to surface fish (Aspiras et al., 2015), and it is possible that prolonged starvation reduces Leptin levels, thereby inhibiting hcrt expression to promote sleep in cavefish.
evidence: Speculative inference based on known Leptin-HCRT interactions and observed effects of starvation.

claim: HCRT neurons are integrators of sleep and metabolic state.
source: In addition to its role in sleep-wake regulation, hcrt neurons regulate feeding and metabolic function, raising the possibility that HCRT neurons are integrators of sleep and metabolic state.
evidence: Inferred from the dual role of HCRT in sleep and feeding regulation and the observed effects of starvation.

claim: Sleep loss in cavefish appears to be an evolved consequence of changes in food availability.
source: Therefore, sleep loss in cavefish appears to be an evolved consequence of changes in food availability, providing a model to examine interactions between sleep and metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that starvation increases sleep in cavefish and the nutrient-poor cave environment.

claim: Sleep is highly pleiotropic and many additional genetic factors likely contribute to sleep differences between sleep in cavefish.
source: Taken together, these studies raise the possibility that evolved differences in HCRT function contribute to the evolution of sleep loss in cavefish. Sleep is highly pleiotropic and it is likely that many additional genetic factors contribute to sleep differences between sleep in cavefish.
evidence: Inference based on the complexity of sleep regulation and the fact that HCRT is only one component.
